title: NAT2 acetylator status and isoniazid
dek: Human NAT2 sets how fast INH is acetylated. Slow acetylators have higher INH exposure and more DILI/neuropathy risk. Rapid acetylators have lower exposure. This is host PK, not katG.
story: Isoniazid is cleared in large part by N-acetylation in the liver, catalysed by N-acetyltransferase 2 (NAT2). Common haplotypes (*5, *6, *7 and others) define slow, intermediate, and rapid acetylator phenotypes. Slow acetylators see higher INH area-under-curve at a given mg/kg dose; rapid acetylators see less.

That PK split shows up as toxicity and, in some studies, as efficacy. Hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy are more common in slow acetylators — which is why pyridoxine and liver monitoring are not optional theatre on HRZE. Some trials of NAT2-guided dosing exist; they are not yet a universal WHO SOP. Standard 5 mg/kg (or 10 mg/kg in children, programme-dependent) remains the labelled starting point unless a protocol says otherwise.
NAT2 is a human gene. It does not sit in the Mtb BAM. A katG S315T story is bacterial activation. A NAT2*6/*6 story is host clearance. Mixing them is how a DST report grows a rs-number.
deepTitle: What a TB programme actually does with this
deep: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) to prevent INH neuropathy, especially in pregnancy, malnutrition, diabetes, HIV, and slow acetylators if known.
DILI: NAT2 is one risk factor among alcohol, PZA, rifampin, viral hepatitis, and pregnancy. The hepatotoxicity plate owns the monitoring grammar.
TPT regimens that are rifamycin-based (3HP, 4R) change the INH burden. NAT2 still matters if INH is in the recipe (3HR, 6H, 1HP).
Do not interpret a low plasma INH level as katG without asking about dose, adherence, and acetylator status.
WGS of the isolate will not call NAT2. Host pharmacogenetics is a different assay.

visual.caption: Human NAT2 coding sequence (schematic cDNA). Star alleles *5 (341T>C), *6 (590G>A), and *7 (857G>A) are the celebrity slow-haplotype SNPs. This track is not H37Rv and not katG.

example.title: Neuropathy on standard INH, katG WT
example.setup: Adult on HRZE, katG/inhA wild type, smear converting. Week 6: stocking-glove neuropathy. Someone wants to add ethionamide “for better INH-effect” and skip B6 because “the genome is INH-S.”

steps.title: This is host PK, not katG
steps.body: INH-S on WGS does not predict NAT2. Slow acetylation plus missing pyridoxine is a classic neuropathy recipe.

steps.title: Do not add a second InhA drug as a reflex
steps.body: Ethionamide is not a B6 substitute and shares neuropathy-adjacent misery. Give pyridoxine, look at dose and alcohol, check HIV and diabetes.

steps.title: If you have NAT2
steps.body: A slow genotype supports the PK story. It still does not belong in the isolate’s DST table.

example.takeaway: NAT2 is human INH clearance. katG is bacterial activation. Pyridoxine is cheaper than a new second-line.

check.prompt: At a fixed INH mg/kg dose, slow acetylators relative to rapid acetylators typically have:
choices: Lower INH exposure and less DILI risk, always
Higher INH exposure and higher risk of DILI/neuropathy
Zero INH in plasma because katG ate it
check.answer: Higher INH exposure and higher risk of DILI/neuropathy
check.why: Slower acetylation, more parent INH. Monitoring and B6 follow.
